textbookText: 11. LYSOSOMES Lysosomes (Gr. Lyso - digestive, soma - body) are microscopic, membrane-bound vesicles within the cytoplasm crucial for intracellular digestion. These pleomorphic structures contain up to 40 types of hydrolytic enzymes, mostly active at pH 5, and digest several biological materials (forming autophagosome), and, sometimes, own cell organelles causing death of the cell (autolysis). Therefore, they are also known as "suicidal bag". Lysosomes were discovered by Belgian biochemist Christian de Duve (1955) within rat liver cells. They are found in most eukaryotic animal cells (excluding mammalian red blood cells), certain fungi (e.g., yeasts), specific protists (e.g., Euglena), and meristematic cells (e.g., root tip cells of maize). Generally, they are spherical but irregular in plant root tip cells.
